Which weapon is better: sword or spear?

Answer: The spear.

I know that the popular answer to this question is “it depends.” And it does depend, in the sense that you can always engineer a scenario in which weapon X is better than weapon Y. It can depend upon the skill of the opposing fencers. It can depend upon the physical, mental, and emotional states of the opposing fencers. It can depend upon the terrain. It can even sometimes depend on which individual example of weapon X and weapon Y you’re talking about. Yes, context matters. Yes, it depends.

But.

Spears are better than swords.

What I mean by that is that there are many more scenarios in which the spear is better than the sword than there are scenarios in which the sword is better than the spear.

Spears hit harder - much harder - than swords. They have significant reach advantages. They are incredibly fast. They can be used with great facility at point blank range (you don’t have to hold the thing at the back, and a long staff is a great wrestling tool). They reward a given amount of skill with a greater amount of effectiveness than do swords.

Even in cramped quarters, the spear is an excellent weapon. For the most part, “cramped quarters” means that the ceiling is low or that there isn’t a lot of clearance from side to side. In this sort of scenario, where you are basically restricted to linear stabbing, the spear is great; in fact, it’s the sword that loses a bunch of its available techniques because there isn’t room to do many cuts. Only when things are so cramped that you literally can’t carry the spear with you anymore do you start running into serious problems.

The one thing that swords unequivocally do better than spears is be worn. You can carry two swords, or a sword and a spear, much more easily than you can carry two spears. You can carry one sword much more easily than you can carry one spear. This is undoubtedly part of why swords have always been more popular than spears as a backup weapon, and as a “civilian carry” weapon.[1] But don’t forget that concern by the authorities over street violence is not a modern phenomenon. People were more uncomfortable with civilian-carry spears than with civilian-carry swords for much the same reason that people are more uncomfortable with civilian-carry shotguns than with civilian-carry pistols: because if somebody decides to start a fight, they can do a lot more damage with the spear or the shotgun than with the sword or the pistol. In a very real sense, swords were acceptable civilian carry because they are essentially bad weapons (Eric Lowe's answer to Aren't swords essentially bad weapons?). Swords are good sidearms, absolutely.[2] But they are not in the same class as spears.[3]

[1] The whole idea of a “civilian,” let alone “civilian carry,” of course, is a very modern phenomenon. I use it deliberately anachronistically, to get across the idea of a weapon worn about town on daily business.

[2] Another way to look at this, in fact, is to ask whether handguns or long guns are better weapons. I think most modern people would intuitively understand that handguns are convenient to carry, don’t arouse as much alarm as long guns when carried in public, etc. - but if you think a handgun is a better weapon than a rifle or a shotgun, you’re crazy.

[3] Except for greatswords. Greatswords are absolutely in the same class as spears, and historically were spoken of in the same breath as polearms quite often.
